summary: An April 1st joke RFC that reformulates IP, TCP and UDP as XML applications under the name Binary Lexical Octet Ad-hoc Transport. It is humor, not a real protocol. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a silly pretend idea for writing network packets in a very wordy format. It was published as an April Fools' joke.

questions: what is binary lexical octet ad-hoc transport
subtitle: An April 1st joke that rewrites IP, TCP and UDP as verbose XML documents and sends them over Ethernet.

tldr.problem: The joke premise is that XML is so popular at the application layer that it should also be used for the network and transport layers.
tldr.mechanism: BLOAT reformulates IPv4, TCP and UDP as XML document types (IPoXML, TCPoXML, UDPoXML), with base-64 payloads, DTDs, Ethernet type 0xBEEF and optional encapsulation in IP.
tldr.outcome: It is an April 1st humor document, not a real protocol, and it is Informational. The behavior of the underlying protocols is unchanged; only the encoding is.

today: RFC 3252 is an Informational April 1st joke, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It was never meant as a real protocol.

sections.title: The Joke: Everything as XML
sections.content:
RFC 3252 was published on 1 April 2002, so it is an April 1st joke document. Played straight-faced, it describes the Binary Lexical Octet Ad-hoc Transport (BLOAT), a reformulation of IP (RFC 791), TCP (RFC 793) and UDP (RFC 768) as XML applications.

The stated motivation is the popularity of XML in application protocols. Using XML at the network and transport layers too would, the RFC claims, give an amazing amount of power and flexibility, let applications use a single XML parser for everything, and remove worries about network versus host byte ordering.

Behavior is meant to stay the same: routing, address spaces and TCP congestion control work as in the existing standards. Only the encoding changes.
sections.plainLanguage: The joke is that someone wants to rewrite the internet's short, tidy messages as long, chatty documents, and claims this makes everything simpler.

sections.title: IPoXML, TCPoXML and UDPoXML
sections.content:
Each protocol becomes an XML document type with its own DTD. The RFC says all three MUST be implemented. Bit-masks become human-readable values, IP addresses are written in dotted-decimal, and length, checksum and port values are decimal integers. IPv4 was chosen over IPv6 because an XML IPv6 would have exceeded the 1500 byte Ethernet MTU.

All implementations MUST use UTF-8 and well-formed documents with the XML declaration. Length and checksum are computed over a canonical form with no whitespace between elements and one space between attributes. Because arbitrary payload bytes do not fit XML, payloads are base-64 encoded as in RFC 2045, without the 76-character line wrapping.

TCP and UDP documents carried inside IPoXML MAY omit the XML header and DOCTYPE. The TCP offset element grows to a maximum of 255 from 16 to allow for the bigger XML header.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a tiny box of numbers, each message is a long form with a labelled line for every detail. Anything that is not text gets translated into letters first.

sections.title: Carrying BLOAT on the Wire
sections.content:
Over Ethernet, BLOAT is framed as in RFC 894, except that the type field MUST contain 0xBEEF. The first 5 octets of the frame payload are 0x3c 3f 78 6d 6c, which spell <?xml. On IEEE 802 networks the protocol type code for IPoXML is also 0xBEEF.

To gateway BLOAT across the public Internet, it MAY be encapsulated in IP as in RFC 2003. The DTDs are named by public and system identifiers, though the RFC admits that fetching a network protocol's DTD over the network is a catch-22, so implementations will normally embed it.
sections.plainLanguage: BLOAT messages ride in the same envelopes as normal ones, just with a silly special stamp number, and can be tunnelled through regular internet mail.

sections.title: Example Datagrams
sections.content:
The RFC gives an example datagram for each protocol, all with empty payloads. The IPoXML example uses version 4, TTL 255 and protocol 6, with a header length of 474 and a total length of 461, and carries source and destination addresses 10.0.0.22 and 10.0.0.1. The TCP and UDP examples use ports 31415 and 42424.

The size of even an empty datagram is the joke: a header that takes 20 bytes in standard IPv4 becomes hundreds of characters of markup. The RFC itself says total length SHOULD be less than 1024 for IPoXML on local Ethernets.
sections.plainLanguage: Even a message with nothing in it fills a whole page of tags and brackets.
